title: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test
subject: Pathology
summary: The OGTT assesses how the body handles a glucose load, identifying normal glucose tolerance, impaired glucose tolerance, and diabetes. It is essential for diagnosing diabetes in pregnancy and for detecting early dysglycaemia in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The Oral Glucose Tolerance Test measures plasma glucose before and after a standardized oral glucose load to evaluate insulin‑mediated glucose disposal.
b: Plasma glucose measured at fasting, 1‑hour and 2‑hour (2‑hour is mandatory)

t.b: Is basal glucose control adequate? – Normal <7.0 mmol/L, diabetes ≥7.0 mmol/L

sections.p: Glycaemic status is staged by the 2‑hour OGTT result, which predicts future risk of overt diabetes and vascular complications.
b: Normal glucose tolerance: 2‑hour <7.8 mmol/L
Impaired glucose tolerance (pre‑diabetes): 2‑hour 7.8‑11.0 mmol/L
Diabetes mellitus: 2‑hour ≥11.1 mmol/L

sections.p: Abnormal OGTT results arise from insulin resistance, beta‑cell failure, or a combination, often precipitated by common regional factors.
b: Type 2 diabetes mellitus – most common, driven by obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and genetics
Gestational diabetes – pregnancy‑induced insulin resistance, screened at 24‑28 weeks
Infections affecting glucose metabolism – HIV (ART‑induced insulin resistance), tuberculosis, malaria (stress hyperglycaemia)
Chronic liver disease (hepatitis B/C) and schistosomiasis – impair gluconeogenesis
Use of corticosteroids, beta‑agonists, or herbal remedies containing steroids

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, or recurrent infections. In pregnancy, excessive fetal growth and polyhydramnios raise suspicion.
b: Polyuria/polydipsia without infection
Unexplained weight loss despite adequate intake
Recurrent genital or skin infections
Large for gestational age fetus or excessive amniotic fluid

sections.p: The OGTT is the cornerstone; adjunct tests help clarify aetiology and complications.
b: If glucose reagents are unavailable, use capillary glucometer with validated strips; interpret with same cut‑offs but note possible bias

t.b: What is chronic glycaemia? – ≥6.5 % confirms diabetes, 5.7‑6.4 % suggests pre‑diabetes
Is hyperinsulinaemia present? – High fasting insulin with normal glucose suggests early insulin resistance

t.a: HIV test, TB screening, malaria smear (regional context)
t.b: Are co‑morbid infections contributing? – Positive results guide additional management

sections.p: Unrecognised or poorly controlled hyperglycaemia can rapidly lead to life‑threatening events, especially in pregnancy.
b: Diabetic ketoacidosis – vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – profound dehydration, altered consciousness
Fetal macrosomia and shoulder dystocia in gestational diabetes
Accelerated atherosclerosis – early coronary or cerebrovascular disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying insulin resistance or beta‑cell failure, then monitor glucose and complications.
b: Lifestyle modification – diet low in refined carbs, regular walking or farming activity, weight reduction if overweight
Metformin (first‑line for type 2 and gestational diabetes when diet fails) – improves insulin sensitivity, cheap and widely available
Insulin therapy for gestational diabetes or when OGTT shows diabetes with fasting >11.1 mmol/L – safe in pregnancy, avoids oral drug teratogenicity
Avoid sulfonylureas in pregnancy (risk of fetal hypoglycaemia) and in patients with renal impairment

sections.p: Regular re‑testing and risk‑factor control reduce progression to overt diabetes and complications.
b: Repeat OGTT every 1‑2 years in women with prior gestational diabetes
Annual fasting glucose or HbA1c in high‑risk adults (obesity, family history, HIV on ART)
Vaccination against hepatitis B and pneumococcus to lower infection‑related hyperglycaemia
Counselling on traditional herbal use that may contain glucocorticoids

sections.p: Conditions that cause transient hyperglycaemia can be mistaken for diabetes.
b: Stress hyperglycaemia from acute infection or trauma – resolves after illness, repeat OGTT after recovery
Cushing’s syndrome – chronic cortisol excess, confirmed by dexamethasone suppression test

sections.p: Certain factors alter OGTT accuracy, especially in low‑resource labs.
b: Recent high‑carbohydrate meal before fasting – may raise fasting glucose falsely
Hemolysed samples – can lower measured glucose
Pregnancy‑induced plasma volume expansion – may dilute glucose, repeat test if borderline

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid breathing (possible ketoacidosis)
Severe dehydration, confusion or unconsciousness (hyperosmolar state)
Rapidly growing fetus with fundal height > gestational age by >2 cm (possible uncontrolled gestational diabetes)

faq.q: Why is the 2‑hour value more important than the fasting value in pregnancy?
faq.a: Pregnancy induces peripheral insulin resistance; post‑load glucose reveals impaired handling that fasting alone may miss.

faq.q: Can a single abnormal OGTT diagnose diabetes?
faq.a: Yes, a 2‑hour glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L meets diagnostic criteria, but repeat testing is advised if the result is unexpected.

exam: A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman at 26 weeks has a fasting glucose of 5.8 mmol/L and a 2‑hour value of 9.0 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis and next step? — Impaired glucose tolerance; advise diet, repeat OGTT at 32 weeks, consider metformin if values rise.

A patient with HIV on efavirenz presents with polyuria. OGTT shows 2‑hour glucose 12.0 mmol/L. How does HIV therapy influence your management? — Recognise ART‑induced insulin resistance; start metformin, review ART regimen, monitor for drug interactions.

A woman with a previous gestational diabetes pregnancy now has a fasting glucose of 6.5 mmol/L but normal 2‑hour value. How do you interpret? — Isolated impaired fasting glucose; advise lifestyle, repeat OGTT in 6 months, consider metformin if progression.
Explain why sulfonylureas are avoided in gestational diabetes. — They cross the placenta and may cause fetal hypoglycaemia; insulin or metformin are safer.

A patient on chronic steroids develops a 2‑hour OGTT of 8.5 mmol/L. What is the likely mechanism and management? — Steroid‑induced insulin resistance; reduce steroid dose if possible, start lifestyle measures, consider metformin.

During a malaria epidemic, many patients have high fasting glucose. How do you differentiate true diabetes from stress hyperglycaemia? — Repeat OGTT after malaria treatment; persistent elevation confirms diabetes.

What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate admission of a patient with newly diagnosed diabetes on OGTT? — Signs of ketoacidosis (vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing) or hyperosmolar state (severe dehydration, altered mental status).
